text:
Graph-Based Predictive and
Prescriptive Analytics for
Cross-Border Power Grid Networks
A reproducible course project that turns messy grid-flow records into explainable forecasts, risk screening, distance-based loss estimates, and stress-aware rerouting scenarios.
PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS · B C S E 3 3 4 L

Opening: frame the project as an auditable decision-support system. The dashboard uses a historical replay of the supplied data. The deck distinguishes measured data, proxy estimates, and engineering validation requirements.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
The project combines a graph view, time-series forecasting, risk classification, and prescriptive what-if analysis in one auditable workflow.
Integration and transparency rather than an unsupported new neural architecture
Canonical edge audit keeps aliases visible and reproducible
Risk score combines flow pressure, imbalance, and load residual
Model router selects the best baseline by chronological RMSE
Stress-aware rerouting exposes bottlenecks instead of hiding infeasibility
The winner is selected by evidence, not by model complexity.
Use this slide as the one-minute overview. The key result is not just the score. The result is the full evidence chain from raw records to a recommendation that retains assumptions and guardrails.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
Why cross-border grid flows are difficult
Power moves across multiple connected areas at once
A single interconnector can become a bottleneck when neighboring links are also busy
Directional records may use inconsistent labels for the same physical link
Observed flow and load signals are time-dependent and can change sign
Physical loss needs voltage, resistance, route length, conductor data, and rating
An operator needs an explanation of why the system flags a link
What should the analyst investigate next?
When observed flow or forecast pressure rises, which interconnector or alternate path deserves attention, and why?
Scope: screening and decision support. Automatic dispatch and switching remain out of scope.
Define the operating problem before showing algorithms. The deck treats the system as a screening tool rather than a certified control system.

Research anchors the design choices. The project applies the useful ideas while avoiding unsupported claims of novelty.
The project’s contribution is an auditable integration of data quality, prediction, physics assumptions, and route testing.
A model score alone does not answer which link to review, whether the inputs are trustworthy, or what a reroute would cost. GridPulse connects those questions in one workflow.
Sources: Li et al. (DCRNN), Wu et al. (Graph WaveNet), 2024 power-system GNN survey, MS-STGNN, 2025 grid-aware STGNN, conformalized load forecasting.

The feature table summarizes results/feature_catalog.json, which contains 11 model inputs. For the loss proxy, the default assumptions are 400 kV, 0.95 PF, copper resistivity 1.68e-8 ohm-m, and 2,000 square millimetres. The dataset does not provide engineering-grade parameters.

How a browser pulse becomes a new screen
The prototype advances one historical hourly snapshot every 2 seconds. A production adapter can replace the replay source with Kafka, MQTT, or utility telemetry while keeping the API shape.

Architecture is intentionally modular. The data pipeline produces compact artifacts so the browser stays responsive. The stream is a historical replay for demonstration, not a utility telemetry connection.

walk forward one hour at a time

Persistence: ŷₜ₊₁ = yₜ

Point estimate plus an adaptive residual band
The selected model is the one with the lowest pooled RMSE. The dashboard adds a residual band that widens with √horizon.
MAPE becomes unstable near zero or when net flow changes sign. MAE, RMSE, and class metrics carry more weight.

The project compares four classical baselines first. That is methodologically defensible because it establishes a leakage-safe benchmark before adding a GNN. Metrics are computed over 2,016 predictions, 12 countries times 168 holdout hours.

Six approaches on one chronological holdout
The saved result pack ranks Fusion GRU first on RMSE. DCRNN keeps the node graph intact, while Fusion GRU uses a global summary context.
Persistence remains the audit baseline: it is cheaper, easier to explain, and useful for checking whether neural graph context adds real value.

This chart reads results/model_comparison.json. The four classical rows come from the existing walk-forward artifact; Fusion GRU and DCRNN come from the same 40-epoch research run with the same 168-hour-per-country test horizon.

Stress classes are Normal, Warning, and Critical
Macro precision, recall, and F1 average the three class-specific values. This prevents the Normal majority class from hiding weak Warning detection.
These metrics classify actual and predicted net-flow magnitudes using country-specific 75th percentile Warning and 90th percentile Critical thresholds derived from the pre-holdout history.
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed

Rows = actual class
Columns = predicted class
Why accuracy alone is not enough
The Warning class is the weakest class because its boundary is harder to separate from Normal behavior. The matrix shows whether the model misses warning episodes or over-alerts.
Formula connection: the per-class values come from TP, FP, and FN counts in this matrix.

This table reads results/confusion_matrix.json generated by the DCRNN experiment. Rows are actual classes and columns are predicted classes. Class thresholds use the 75th and 90th percentiles of the training magnitude.

A transparent bridge from coordinates to a screening estimate

S = |P| / pf
I = S / (√3 · V)
P_loss = 3 · I² · R
Assumptions: 400 kV · PF 0.95 · copper ρ = 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m · A = 2,000 mm²
Engineering-grade loss remains unavailable because the dataset lacks surveyed corridors, conductor construction, thermal ratings, reactive power, and actual voltage.

This slide is intentionally explicit about the boundary between physics education and operational engineering. The proxy uses country-centroid distance and assumed constants. Replace the assumptions when verified line data becomes available.

A route is a screening result, not an operating command
If no complete path meets guardrails, the UI reports BEST EFFORT and names the bottleneck edges.

The live interface computes a shortest path over the visible graph. Its hard conditions are proxy headroom and critical-state avoidance. The route planner can return route_found, best_effort_only, no_alternate_path, or no_change.

What the project must not overclaim
Historical replay, not live utility telemetry
Capacity is an observed-flow proxy, not a thermal rating
Loss uses centroid distance and assumed constants
No voltage stability or N-1 power-flow solver
DCRNN is a benchmark, not proof of engineering superiority
Experiments that would strengthen the research
Add verified line geometry, conductor, voltage, and capacity data
Extend the completed DCRNN benchmark with GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE
Add conformal uncertainty with coverage evaluation
Run ablations across topology, weather, and quality flags
Validate route recommendations in an engineering solver
Bottom line: the project delivers a credible, explainable prototype and a clear path to engineering-grade research.
Close with the boundary. The project is strong because it makes uncertainty and missing engineering data visible. The future work list turns those limitations into experiments.

A single example at one country
Fusion GRU receives 24 hourly steps and combines local, network, and static graph signals

mean flow · load
mean stress signals

Example reading: if DE has a high recent flow but neighboring countries show stable load and imbalance, the GRU can retain the local pressure while using the network context to moderate the prediction.
The neural model is judged by holdout evidence

Fusion GRU
RMSE 570.5 MW
MAE 400.3 MW
The gates do not make a forecast from a single feature. They learn when to keep recent memory and when to update it with a new graph-and-demand pattern.
Training target: next-hour country net flow
Fusion GRU is the local-plus-global sequence model. The example is explanatory, while the displayed metrics come from the saved 40-epoch run. The model is not a dispatch controller.

title: HOW GRAPH DIFFUSION CHANGES THE FORECAST

Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
DCRNN passes a node's signal through neighboring interconnectors before the recurrent update

DE's input can receive
forward and reverse
neighbor context
The same 24-hour window is processed at each time step
Start with each country's current features
Move information one graph step at a time
Dₜ = [Xₜ, P Xₜ, P² Xₜ, Pᵀ Xₜ, (Pᵀ)² Xₜ]
Concatenate self, two forward steps, and two reverse steps
Saved DCRNN result: RMSE 634.0 MW · macro-F1 83.8%

DCRNN uses two row-normalized transition matrices: forward and reverse walks over the 24 canonical links. The model preserves the node dimension instead of replacing the graph with one global average. The displayed result is the actual run from results/dcrnn_analysis.json.

title: WHY GRAPH CONTEXT DID NOT WIN THIS RUN

text: WHY GRAPH CONTEXT DID NOT WIN THIS RUN
Source: supplied CSVs and reproducible artifacts in data/processed
RMSE lower is better; macro-F1 higher is better
RMSE bars are divided by 2,000 only so both scales fit in one editable chart. The table and labels above retain the original units.
Why DCRNN trails Fusion GRU here
A result is useful when it explains the boundary of the method
DCRNN RMSE is 634.0 MW versus Fusion GRU 570.5 MW
The graph is only 12 nodes and 24 links, so diffusion adds limited new information beyond global context
The data has no verified ratings, dispatch constraints, market shocks, or route geometry
Persistence remains hard to beat because hourly flow is strongly autocorrelated
The model is slower and more complex, so it needs more evidence before operational use
Conclusion: graph diffusion is implemented and measured. It is not automatically the winner.

This slide uses results/model_comparison.json and results/dcrnn_analysis.json. The conclusion is deliberately bounded: DCRNN is a real benchmark, but this dataset and feature set do not provide enough evidence to prefer it over Fusion GRU or the operational Persistence baseline.
